title: Candidate handoff — uncertainty map
content:
Candidate: Jonah Park — Senior Runtime Engineer candidate; onsite loop: system design + live-coding + take-home review

Quick gist / gut: strong product sense for inference platform tradeoffs, confident with latency/cost thinking. Technical depth uneven: good on throughput/batching heuristics and practical kernel tradeoffs, weaker on implementation details for KV cache eviction and memory profiling. Culture fit seems high (asks good infra questions).

Interview narrative (rough timeline):
- 30m intro / past projects: Jonah talked through building a custom inference edge for a previous company — emphasized ops automation and cost-per-token reductions via batching and cache. Clear ownership examples (oncall rotations, perf incident runs).
- 1hr system design: designed an autoscaling + fallback policy for an LLM endpoint that could degrade gracefully between GPU types. Good conceptual routing: region-aware, model-variant fallback, explicit capacity tiers. Skipped some API-level failure scenarios and didn't quantify SLOs beyond rough latency percentiles.
- 45m live-coding: implemented simplified prefix caching API in Python. Code quality okay, but left out concurrent request handling and memory limits; needed prompting on race conditions.
- Take-home discussion: had a thoughtful retrospective and clear metrics (p50/p95 cost delta). Implementation was pragmatic but used higher-level libraries rather than low-level memory ops.

Signals (what I noticed):
- Positive:
  - Operational thinking: very used to measuring unit cost and tradeoffs (batch size vs latency vs throughput).
  - Product/CS empathy: prioritized predictable degradation pathways and customer-facing SLAs.
  - Clear ownership: concrete examples of running incidents and postmortems.

- Neutral / mixed:
  - Familiarity with quantization: conceptual (aware of 4-bit/8-bit tradeoffs) but hasn't implemented custom kernel changes. Could learn but may need support for model-flavor onboarding.
  - Autoscaling instincts good, but lacked hard numbers in the design (no capacity calc for cold start amplification or GPU packing).

- Red flags / uncertainties:
  - Concurrency & memory management: during live-coding they deferred on eviction strategy and didn't demonstrate experience writing safe concurrent shared-memory code. On a high-throughput runtime we'd want that skill.
  - Low-level performance tuning: limited systems-level profiling examples (perf, nvprof-like workflows). Past role leaned on infra team for kernel-level changes.

Uncertainty map (what I'm least certain about and why):
- KV cache eviction across multi-tenant workloads: candidate confident in cache policies conceptually (LRU, TTL, golden tokens) but hasn't designed eviction strategies that account for mixed-priority tenants and bursty tails. This is an important production gap.
- Quantization/compiled-kernel troubleshooting: they know the landscape but haven't debugged kernel correctness/perf regressions before. Risk: longer ramp to own model onboarding for exotic quantized variants.
- Concurrency at kernel boundary (CUDA / ucx / shared GPU memory): didn't show examples of having implemented and tested race-free code at this level. Unclear if they'd be comfortable owning that stack immediately.

Suggested follow-ups (concrete asks if we move forward):
1) Short assignment: give Jonah a small bug/PR that touches concurrent access to an in-memory KV cache (4–8h). Look for explicit locking strategy, tests for races, and memory safety notes.
2) Ask for a 1–page note on how they'd do eviction for a multi-tenant inference host (metrics to track, SLO-driven decisions, fallback behavior). This will reveal operational detail depth.
3) If passing, pair with a senior infra engineer on a 90m deep-dive (kernel/quant path) to surface how they'd ask questions and learn.

Tentative score (on our rubric):
- System design: 7/10 (good high-level design, missing SLO quantification)
- Coding (concurrency + correctness): 5.5/10 (works in higher-level code, concurrency gaps)
- Production ownership: 8/10 (strong incident ownership and product thinking)
- Low-level perf/quant: 5/10 (conceptual knowledge but lacks hands-on experience)

Overall recommendation: move to contrived final stage only if they complete the short assignment (concurrency PR) satisfactorily. I like the candidate for a runtime team oriented toward product and ops improvements, but we need to validate low-level concurrency and quantization ramp ability.

Notes to self / micro-actions before handing off to hiring committee:
- Add Jonah's LinkedIn + GH link to the packet and highlight the PR we referenced (linked_artifacts above).
- Flag for interviewers: emphasize memory-safety, kernel debugging, and ask for numbers in design questions.
- If we decide to pass, schedule a 30m follow-up specifically with an SRE-level interviewer focused on memory profiling and race detection tools.

Loose thoughts (stream-of-consciousness extras):
- Candidate's time-to-ramp might be shorter in teams that already encapsulate kernel work behind a stable runtime (e.g., Redwood runtime team could pair them with someone senior on quant).
- Might be a great hire for a role owning batching/caching and customer-facing performance SLAs rather than raw kernel hacking.

End of notes.
